question: A 15-year-old teenager presents for a sports physical. His blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), and heart rate is 100/min. On cardiac auscultation, an early diastolic heart sound is heard over the cardiac apex while the patient is in the left lateral decubitus position. A transthoracic echocardiogram is performed which shows an ejection fraction of 60% without any other abnormalities. Which of the following is the end-systolic volume in this patient if his cardiac output is 6 L/min?

enhanced_information: To determine the end-systolic volume (ESV) in this patient, we use the formula: Ejection Fraction (EF) = (Stroke Volume (SV) / End-Diastolic Volume (EDV)) * 100. Given the cardiac output is 6 L/min and heart rate is 100/min, the stroke volume is calculated as 60 mL (6000 mL/min divided by 100/min). The ejection fraction is given as 60%, which means 60% of the end-diastolic volume is ejected per beat. Rearranging the EF formula gives us: SV = EF * EDV. Solving for EDV gives EDV = SV / (EF/100) = 60 mL / 0.6 = 100 mL. The end-systolic volume is then EDV - SV = 100 mL - 60 mL = 40 mL. Therefore, the correct end-systolic volume is 40 mL, aligning with standard cardiac physiology.
